Endangered languages. Languages with so few remaining speakers that they face extinction within one to three generations. As globalization, urbanization, and dominant-language education policies accelerate language shift, linguists estimate that roughly half of the world's approximately seven thousand languages will disappear by the year twenty-one hundred. The loss of an endangered language erases not only a unique communication system but also irreplaceable knowledge systems, cultural practices, and worldviews embedded in that language.

Language extinction accelerates during periods of rapid cultural change. Colonial conquest, industrialization, and now digital globalization have each triggered mass language death. The number of speakers does not correlate exactly with extinction risk. Factors include intergenerational transmission—whether children still learn the language at home—community prestige, and whether speakers value their language, and access to education. Endangered languages are not uniformly distributed. Indigenous and minority languages in the Americas, Africa, Asia-Pacific, and Eurasia bear the highest extinction burden. The Americas alone account for roughly forty percent of global linguistic diversity.

Documentation of endangered languages—audio recordings, grammatical descriptions, and digital archives—has become a critical intervention. Linguists race to preserve linguistic data before speakers pass away. The extinction of a language often coincides with loss of ecological knowledge, oral history, ritual practice, and identity. The Basque and Maltese languages survived political suppression partly through deliberate cultural revival efforts.

Language-death processes vary. Some languages fade gradually as bilingual speakers shift to the dominant language. Others vanish abruptly after traumatic events like colonization, genocide, or forced assimilation. Endangered-language communities often experience structural inequalities. Marginalized speakers lack economic incentive to transmit the language, while dominant-language schooling actively discourages it.
